opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair critique, and I think it's one people should take seriously. If you just look at it naively, you're doing these enormous rollouts, thousands of tokens of generation, and at the end you get back basically one scalar: did it work or didn't it. Compared to pretraining, where every single token gives you a dense gradient signal, that looks incredibly wasteful on a bits-per-FLOP basis.

But I think the framing misses what that signal is actually doing. Pretraining teaches the model a huge amount about the world, but it's learning to imitate the distribution of what people wrote. RL is the thing that teaches the model what *it* should do, given its own capabilities, in its own situations. That's a very different kind of information. A small number of bits that say "this whole strategy, the way you approached the problem, the way you recovered from your mistake, that worked" can be enormously valuable, because they're shaping behavior in a way imitation just can't. You can't really learn to recover from your own errors by watching other people not make them.

The other thing is that RL isn't creating capabilities from nothing. It's mostly selecting and sharpening things that are already latent in the base model. So you don't need a ton of bits, you need the right bits. You're kind of steering a very capable system toward the behaviors you want, and steering doesn't take that much information if the thing you're steering is already powerful.

That said, I do think there's a lot of room to make it more efficient, and that's where a lot of the interesting work is. Better reward design, richer feedback than just pass/fail, rubrics, process-level signals, environments that give you intermediate information, better credit assignment across long trajectories. Also just being smarter about which problems you train on, so you're spending compute in the zone where the model sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails, because that's where the gradient actually has information in it. If it always gets it right or always gets it wrong, you're burning compute for nothing.

So I'd say: yes, it's expensive per bit, but the bits are unusually high-leverage, and the practical question is less "is RL worth it" and more "how do we build environments and rewards that make every rollout count." That's increasingly where I think the field's effort should go.

r001.rationale: The response says RL uses compute to steer and sharpen behaviors, but does not explain that increased compute can substitute for additional human training data.

r002.rationale: The response discusses steering latent capabilities and improving feedback, but does not identify exploration as a way to improve a model when no larger model is available to distill from.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the information-theoretic framing is right but it's also a little bit of a trap, because it makes it sound like RL is a worse version of pretraining when really it's doing a different job. In pretraining you get a dense signal, every token is a target, and that's great for cramming knowledge in. But the thing you're actually buying with RL isn't knowledge, it's something closer to calibration of behavior. You already have a model that knows how to do the task in some latent sense, it just doesn't reliably choose to do it. And a bit or two of signal per episode turns out to be enough to shift which of those behaviors gets expressed, because you're not teaching it from scratch, you're selecting among things it can already do.

The other piece is that the compute isn't really wasted the way it looks on paper. Most of that compute is inference, it's rollouts, and rollouts are the model exploring. If you think of the samples as the model generating its own curriculum, then the sparse reward is just the filter at the end. The expensive part is producing candidates, and the cheap part is deciding which ones were good. That's a very different cost structure than supervised learning, and it's one where the returns are gated on how good your verifier or environment is rather than how much human data you can find. So when people say RL is sample-inefficient, I kind of want to say, inefficient with respect to what? With respect to labeled human data it's incredibly efficient, because you basically need none of it.

Where I think the critique does land is that if your reward signal is noisy or gameable, you're spending all that compute to learn the wrong thing very confidently. The small signal problem is really a signal quality problem. So a lot of the work right now, honestly, is less about the algorithm and more about building environments where the one bit you get back actually means what you think it means. If you get that right, the compute math looks fine. If you get it wrong, no amount of GPUs saves you.

r001.rationale: It says RL uses rollout compute to improve behavior while requiring essentially no labeled human data, explaining how compute can replace additional human training data.

r002.rationale: It describes rollouts as exploration and self-generated curriculum, but does not connect this to improving a model when no larger model is available to distill from.

astra-6.text:
I think the important question is what that signal lets you learn, rather than just how many bits you get per unit of compute. A reward might only tell you whether an answer was right or wrong, but if you couldn’t already produce the right answer reliably, that feedback can be pretty valuable.

There’s a real efficiency concern, though. You might generate a long rollout and get one scalar back, and then you have to figure out which decisions actually mattered. If you have good demonstrations, learning from those can be a much more direct way to make progress.

What makes reinforcement learning interesting is that you don’t necessarily need someone to demonstrate the solution. You need a way to check it. If checking a solution is easier than finding one, you can spend compute searching for successful behavior and then train the model to produce that behavior more reliably. So I’d judge it by how much useful capability you get out of that process. A small information signal can still be worth a lot if it’s a signal you couldn’t otherwise get.

r001.rationale: The response says RL can use compute to search for successful behavior without someone demonstrating the solution, then train the model on that behavior. This clearly presents compute as an alternative to additional demonstrations.

r002.rationale: The response describes searching for successful behavior, but does not identify the specific case where no larger model is available to distill from.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between how much information you get and how useful that information is. A reward might be a single bit—did this work or not?—but if it lets you distinguish a good trajectory from a bad one on a problem you care about, that can be a very valuable bit.

The model is also not learning from scratch from that signal. Pretraining has already given it a huge amount of structure. Reinforcement learning can help it use what it knows more effectively: which approaches to try, when to check its work, when to keep going. So a small amount of feedback can change behavior quite substantially.

That doesn’t mean the compute cost is irrelevant. If you can get the same improvement with good demonstrations, you should probably do that. But there are problems where recognizing a successful outcome is much easier than writing down the steps to get there. That’s where reinforcement learning becomes particularly compelling. You can spend compute searching for solutions and then turn the successful attempts into an improvement in the model. The question is whether that improvement is worth the cost, rather than whether the reward itself contains many bits.
